prime.problem: The image service's queue must fail over automatically: a human is too slow for 99.9%, and a backup that promotes itself on silence creates two leaders during a partition. You need a group of servers that agrees on one leader and one log, never loses a committed entry, and keeps going while a majority is up.
prime.fits: Builds on the service-discovery card's majority quorums and the quorums card's overlap argument; it's the "Paxos leader election" the architecture card relied on. This is the coordination the consistency part says to use only for the rules a merge can break.
expect: terms and randomised election timeouts (150–300 ms)
commit on a majority, own-term entries only
prime.goal: Trace an election after a leader crash, explain why a lagging node can't win and why nothing committed is lost, and put numbers on failover time and per-commit latency.

attend: Why did S5 and S4 each start an election and lose, and what exactly did S2 and S3 check before refusing?
Why does randomising the election timeout matter, and what happens if every timeout is exactly 150 ms?
How does the new leader repair S5's log that is two entries behind?
Why does S3 append a no-op for term 4 before counting anything as committed?
Why does a commit in a five-node group spread over four regions wait 69 ms, not 8 ms?

must: Leader silent past a follower's randomised timeout → it becomes a candidate for a new term and asks for votes → one vote per server per term, granted only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date → a majority elects one leader per term

An entry is committed once a majority stores it → any two majorities overlap (2q − n ≥ 1) → every winning coalition includes someone holding every committed entry, who refuses candidates that lack it → the new leader always has every committed entry
The leader replicates with AppendEntries carrying the previous entry → a follower missing it says no → the leader steps back one index and retries → logs are repaired to match the leader's

A commit waits for the leader plus q − 1 acks → latency = the (q − 1)-th fastest follower RTT (69 ms for 5 nodes from East US) → and with no majority reachable, writes stop: consensus picks consistency over availability
elevated: A leader counts replicas only for entries from its own term → so it appends a no-op on election → committing that no-op commits all earlier entries with it → without the rule, an old-term entry on a majority could still be overwritten
reference: the 10,000-seed table (44.2%, 217 ms mean, 450 ms p99)
ZAB vs Raft vs Paxos naming; etcd and Consul as implementations

compress.prompt: From memory, write Raft as three chains: election (timeout → candidate → votes with the up-to-date check → leader), replication (append → majority → commit, own term only), safety (majorities overlap → committed entries survive). Put one number on each.
checklist: randomised timeouts avoid split votes (150–300 ms)
one vote per term, only for an up-to-date log
commit = stored on a majority; the leader counts only its own term's entries (hence the no-op)
AppendEntries repairs followers by stepping back to the last matching entry
two majorities share a server, so committed entries can't be lost
every write pays the majority's round trip; no majority → no writes

retrieve.q: Explain why S4, one entry behind, could never become leader after S1 crashed, using the overlap argument.
answer: entry 4 is on S1, S2, S3 (a majority), so it is committed
any 3 votes must include S1, S2 or S3; S1 is down
S2 and S3 refuse any candidate whose log lacks entry 4, so S4's best is S4 + S5 = 2 of 5

retrieve.q: Walk through the log repair for S5 (log [1, 1]) after S3 becomes leader with [1, 1, 1, 1, 4].
answer: S3 sends AppendEntries for index 5 with prev = 4: S5 has no entry 4, says no
S3 sends entries 3, 4, 5; S5's log becomes [1, 1, 1, 1, 4]
once index 5 is on 4 of 5 servers (≥ 3), commitIndex = 5, committing 1–5

retrieve.q: Should the image service run a 5-node Raft group across four regions, or a 3-node group in one region, for its job queue? Give the cost and the gain of each.
answer: 5 nodes across regions: each commit waits the 2nd-fastest follower RTT, 69 ms (13.8% of the 500 ms budget); survives a region loss
3 nodes in one region: commits in under 10 ms; a region-wide event takes the queue down
for the job queue, the per-job commit is paid 10K times a second, which favours one region plus the correlated-failure card's work on c

compare.q: Both use majorities, but a Dynamo-style store with w = r = 2 of 3 can still return an old value under LWW, and Raft can't. Which design choice makes the difference?
answer: Raft has one leader per term that orders every write in one log; there are no concurrent versions to pick between
the quorum store lets any replica accept writes, so it must choose a winner by timestamp, and clocks skew
the price: Raft needs a leader election on failure and refuses writes without a majority

compare.q: In CAP terms, what does a Raft group do on each side of a partition that splits 5 nodes into 3 and 2, and why is that not a contradiction of "highly available"?
answer: the 3-node side elects a leader (if needed) and keeps committing
the 2-node side can't get a majority: it refuses writes
CAP's A requires every non-failing node to answer, so this is CP; operators call it highly available because the majority side stays up

predict.q: The old leader S1 restarts after S3 has become leader of term 4. S1 still believes it leads term 1 and sends AppendEntries to S2. What happens to S1's message, and what happens to S1? Commit first.
predict.answer: S2 is in term 4, so it rejects an AppendEntries from term 1 and replies with its current term. S1 sees a higher term (4 > 1), steps down to follower and adopts term 4. From then on it accepts S3's AppendEntries, and its log gets index 5 (the term-4 no-op) appended. Terms are what stop a returning old leader from causing split brain.
